frontier model.definition: An AI model near the leading edge of general capability at the time it is assessed.
frontier model.analogy: The fastest cars on the current starting grid; the lineup changes.

agent.definition: An AI system that can choose and carry out steps using tools toward a goal.
agent.analogy: An assistant who can take actions, rather than only give advice.

alignment.definition: How well an AI system’s behavior matches the intentions and values it is meant to follow.
alignment.analogy: Following both the request and its purpose.

misalignment.definition: Behavior that departs from the goals or constraints the system is intended to follow.
misalignment.analogy: Finishing the assigned job in a way the person who asked would reject.

reward hacking.definition: Getting a high training score through a loophole rather than doing the intended task.
reward hacking.analogy: Winning a step-count contest by shaking the tracker.

scheming.definition: Strategically concealing actions or objectives in order to pursue a goal that conflicts with oversight.
scheming.analogy: Appearing to follow a rule while planning around it. A hypothesis about behavior, not a claim of consciousness.

monitorability.definition: How well observers can notice and understand important AI behavior, including potentially harmful actions.
monitorability.analogy: Having a useful flight recorder and someone who can interpret it in time.

model weights.definition: The learned numerical parameters that determine much of how a model responds.
model weights.analogy: The stored settings shaped by training, rather than a list of explicit instructions.

inference.definition: Running a trained model to produce an output.
inference.analogy: Using a learned skill after practice is over.

reinforcement learning.definition: Training that encourages actions associated with higher feedback scores or rewards.
reinforcement learning.analogy: Practicing with feedback about which attempts worked better.

recursive self-improvement.definition: A proposed feedback loop in which improvements to an AI system help it make further improvements to itself.
recursive self-improvement.analogy: A toolmaker building better tools that then help build even better tools. This is stronger than merely using AI to write code.

context window.definition: The amount of information a model can work with at once in an interaction.
context window.analogy: The papers that fit on a desk, not everything in the library.

zero-day.definition: A software vulnerability for which defenders have no available fix when it is first exploited or disclosed.
zero-day.analogy: An unknown weakness in a lock before a repair is available.

tool use.definition: An AI calling an external capability, such as a calculator, search tool, or code runner.
tool use.analogy: Reaching for a tool instead of answering from memory.

exfiltration.definition: Moving information out of a system without authorization.
exfiltration.analogy: Taking documents out through an unapproved exit.

containment.definition: Controls that limit an AI system’s access to outside systems, data, or resources.
containment.analogy: A controlled workspace with restricted doors and equipment.

sandbox.definition: A restricted computing environment intended to limit what a program can access or change.
sandbox.analogy: A practice room with boundaries. A sandbox escape crosses a boundary the designers intended to enforce.

CBRN.definition: Chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear risks.
CBRN.analogy: A broad group of high-consequence hazards; an AI test score is not a real-world harmful outcome.
